claims.text: Stringfield's anonymised letter-number case coding is the structural reason the retrieval corpus resists tier-1 verification: the coding was designed to protect sources from precisely the security apparatus whose existence the corpus asserts, and it succeeded, at the cost of making the corpus unauditable. Reasoning: the codes are internally consistent across seven reports but map to no released personnel record.

label: Leonard H. Stringfield
narrative: Leonard H. Stringfield (1920-1994) is the origin point of the crash-retrieval literature as a body of work rather than a rumour. A former Army Air Forces intelligence officer in the Pacific in World War II, he founded CRIFO (Civilian Research, Interplanetary Flying Objects) in Cincinnati in the 1950s and served 1967-1969 as an Early Warning Coordinator feeding sighting reports to the Condon Committee, which put him inside the official investigative loop before he turned on it. After references to crashes and recovered bodies in his 1977 Doubleday book 'Situation Red, The UFO Siege' produced an unexpected flow of new informants, he delivered 'Retrievals of the Third Kind: A Case Study of Alleged UFOs and Occupants in Military Custody' at the ninth annual MUFON Symposium in Dayton, Ohio, on 29 July 1978. That paper opened the modern retrieval literature and he then produced six further Status Reports between January 1980 and February 1994, each a numbered, dated, case-coded compilation of testimony from sources he anonymised behind letter-number codes. His method is the load-bearing weakness and the load-bearing strength of the whole field: he protected sources absolutely, which is why they talked to him, and which is also why almost nothing he published can be independently audited. Stringfield himself said so, opening Status Report IV with a section titled 'The Burden of Proof' in which he wrote that 'we, in the domain of public research, do not have that exalted proof' and that affidavits, leaked documents and photographs do not constitute proof. He worked with the Fund for UFO Research, MUFON, CUFOS and the Mid-Ohio Research Associates, and Richard Hall edited Status Report VI. He died of lung cancer on 18 December 1994, ten months after the last report.
